title: Cross-node allreduce latency hunt and scaling playbook
content:
Summary:
This working note records a focused investigation into cross-node communication latency impacting multi-GPU parallelism for inference serving. We observed that for medium-length sequences (512-1024 tokens) and small to moderate batch sizes (1-8), throughput regresses as we add more GPUs across nodes. Hypothesis: all-reduce and NCCL collectives are dominating tail latency due to interconnect saturation and suboptimal group sizing; secondary causes include suboptimal kernel overlap, CPU-to-GPU copy stalls, and noisy NIC/driver configuration.

Goals:
- Determine the primary root cause(s) for cross-node throughput degradation.
- Establish a repeatable microbenchmark and profiler pipeline to measure comms vs compute bottlenecks.
- Produce short, prescriptive mitigations (config knobs, group sizing heuristics, batching guidance).

Environment (baseline):
- Model: Transformer decoder-only variant, 6.7B params, FP16, KV cache enabled
- HW: 2 nodes x 8x A100-40GB (NVLInk within node), Mellanox HDR200/100Gbps InfiniBand between nodes
- OS/driver: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA 535.x drivers, CUDA 12.1, NCCL 2.18
- Framework: PyTorch 2.2, torch.distributed with torchrun
- Serving runtime: local experiment harness built from serving-runtime/bench/runner.py (linked in PR)

Quick reproduction commands:
(1) nccl-tests allreduce microbenchmark
- git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests && make -j
- mpirun -np 16 --host nodeA:8,nodeB:8 \
  -x NCCL_DEBUG=INFO -x NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 \
  build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 8G -f 2 -g 8

(2) simple model throughput (torchrun)
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0 NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0 \
  python -m torch.distributed.run --nproc_per_node=8 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=0 \
  serving_runtime/bench/run_inference.py --model-size=6.7B --seq-len=512 --batch=4 --tokens=1024 --iters=200

Data to capture:
- wall-clock throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p90/p99 latency per token
- GPU utilization (nvidia-smi dmon or DCGM), GPU PCIe bandwidth counters (nvidia-smi --query), NVLink utilization (nvlink_stats), GPU SM active time
- IB utilization: perfquery/ibstat or Mellanox pm tool output; NIC counters (rx/tx bandwidth, CFR drops)
- NCCL traces: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs, timestamps for each collective
- Host-side: dmesg/syslog for driver interrupts, CPU steal, IRQ balancing

Observed microbenchmark results (summary):
- nccl-tests all_reduce_perf: collective latency per-byte grows non-linearly after 4 nodes; bandwidth per-GPU drops ~18% when moving from 4 to 8 nodes for 8 GPUs/node config.
- Application runs: tokens/sec drops ~22% when scaling from 8 to 16 GPUs across nodes, while intra-node scaling (1->8 GPUs on a single node) shows near-linear scaling.
- NCCL logs show frequent retries and timeouts on large messages (~>16MB per allreduce).

Initial hypotheses (ranked):
1) Inter-node IB link saturation for the pattern of large KV cache synchronizations causes per-step stalls. Evidence: NIC counters spike during collective windows and match reduction in measured throughput.
2) NCCL algorithm choice and root selection for AllReduce is suboptimal for our message sizes; fallback to tree-based algorithms increases latency for our topology.
3) Host CPU process imbalance or IRQs cause delayed progress, especially with small batch sizes where host-to-device scheduling overhead is significant.
4) NVLink intra-node is efficient, but cross-node aggregation lacks overlap (compute not overlapping with comms) because tensor layout forces synchronous collectives.

Notes from profiler traces:
- Using nsight systems and NCCL traces, we see 60-80ms windows where GPUs are idle waiting on NCCL ops immediately after kernel launches. Kernel execution time is short (5-20ms) but wait time is large when collectives occur.
- PCIe counters show bursts but average PCIe throughput is well below saturation; suggests that the bottleneck is the IB network rather than CPU<->GPU copies.

Mitigation strategies (short list):
A) Reduce frequent large collectives: shard KV cache and avoid global allreduce on every step. Introduce staggered sync (rotate which ranks sync each step) to flatten IB usage.
B) Tune NCCL env vars: NCCL_TOPO_FILE for topology-aware algorithms, NCCL_ALGO=TREE/RING based on message size experiments, NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=0/1 for testing.
C) Enable async overlap: restructure code to kick off NCCL ops as non-blocking streams and schedule compute on independent CUDA streams. Ensure progress threads are not starved (set NCCL_PROGRESS_THREAD=1).
D) Adjust parallel group sizing: prefer smaller tensor-parallel groups to reduce per-collective message sizes; use pipeline parallelism to trade compute for smaller comms.
E) IB config: set MTU, ensure SR-IOV/Flow control is tuned; test enabling/disabling GPU Direct RDMA path, verify OS level IRQ affinity.
F) grpc/worker pacing: in the serving runtime, add micro-delay when combining requests into a batch to better align compute/comms windows and avoid synchronized spikes.

Experiment matrix (prioritized):
1) nccl-tests sweep: message sizes [1KB, 64KB, 1MB, 16MB], algorithms [RING,TREE], nodes [1,2,4]. Capture per-run latency and BW.
2) Torch model runs: measure tokens/sec while toggling NCCL_ALGO and NCCL_P2P_DISABLE, and with/without NCCL_PROGRESS_THREAD=1.
3) Shard KV sync test: implement a proof-of-concept where only a subset of ranks exchange KV each step and measure throughput/quality regression.
4) Async overlap proof: modify runner to use non-blocking collectives and measure idle GPU time windows.

Representative command snippets to toggle NCCL behavior:
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_ALGO=RING NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0 python -m torch.distributed.run ...
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_ALGO=TREE NCCL_DEBUG_SUPPORTED=1 NCCL_PROGRESS_THREAD=1 ...

Early experiment outcomes (notes):
- Switching NCCL_ALGO to RING lowered p99 latencies for 16MB messages by ~12% on 2-node tests, but increased CPU usage.
- Enabling NCCL_PROGRESS_THREAD removed some stalls on nodes with many processes, improving tokens/sec ~6% in long-running runs.
- Sharded-KV reduced IB instantaneous utilization spikes by ~35% and restored ~14% of tokens/sec in 2-node runs, but requires careful correctness checks for stale KV reads.

Operational checklist for staging rollout (if mitigations are accepted):
- Add nccl microbenchmark to daily infra smoke tests; fail if cross-node allreduce latency exceeds threshold for key message sizes.
- Expose a small set of NCCL env vars in dedicated clusters via runtime config (NCCL_ALGO, NCCL_PROGRESS_THREAD, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME) and document recommended defaults.
- Add an option in serving-runtime config to enable staggered KV sync and validate model fidelity on a representative eval set.
- Update runbooks with commands to collect NIC counters and NCCL logs for on-call triage.

Open questions / unknowns:
- What is the cost to model quality when using stale or partial KV sync compared to throughput gains? Need A/B eval.
- Will smaller tensor-parallel groups materially increase memory pressure per-GPU beyond our 40GB budgets? Run memory-pressure tests.
- Are there firmware/driver updates planned for our Mellanox NICs that target this workload pattern? Coordinate with infra.

Next steps (action items with owners):
- Finish nccl-tests sweep and attach plots (Marco) — due 2024-11-08.
- Prototype sharded-KV in bench harness and run cross-node correctness tests (Nina) — due 2024-11-12.
- Add NCCL env var matrix to CI staging and run overnight smoke (Jamal) — due 2024-11-10.
- Write short runbook on how to capture NCCL and IB counters for oncall (Priya) — due 2024-11-15.

Appendix: quick diagnostics cheat-sheet
- If tokens/sec drops only when adding nodes but not when adding GPUs intra-node: likely interconnect issue.
- Check 'ibstat' + 'perfquery' during a stressed run. High ib bandwidth with packet drops => flow-control/mtu or link-level issue.
- NCCL_DEBUG=INFO logs: look for 'transport: ret=-X' or 'collNetSync' warnings.
- Use 'nvprof/nsys' to confirm idle GPU windows line up with NCCL ops.

This doc is a living working note. Add experiment outputs, csvs, and plots as attachments or links in linked_artifacts as we iterate.
